newsitem.title: Czech republic: CZECH PARLT SENDS BUDGET AHEAD ON CLIFFHANGER VOTE.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PARLT SENDS BUDGET AHEAD ON CLIFFHANGER VOTE.

text.p: The Czech parliament on Wednesday gave the minority centre-right coalition a key victory, approving the first reading of the government's draft 1997 balanced budget, as four opposition deputies broke party ranks.
The 103 to 95 vote with two absentions locks in the principal budget totals for the final two readings in the lower house although details can be changed or the entire packgage can still be rejected.
The draft, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's fifth straight balanced budget plan, proposes equal revenue and expenditure of 549.1 billion crowns next year.
Klaus's coalition had hinted that it might resign if the opposition succeeded in forcing changes to the budget.

Traditionally the third and final reading of the budget comes in December, but inconclusive elections in June put Klaus's government two votes shy of a majority in parliament and put the 1997 budget process in doubt.

The government won the crucial first reading when four Social Democrats -- including budget committee chairman Jozef Wagner and deputy party chairman Karel Machovec -- crossed party lines to vote with the coalition.
Wagner also voted with the coalition to kill a series of Social Democrat proposals earlier on Wednesday which would have forced the government budget draft to be partly rewritten.
Klaus earlier on Wednesday praised Wagner amid signs that an opposition split could hand the government victory.
Wagner had told parliament on Tuesday that although he disagreed with the government on many things, the budget needed to be passed for the stability of the country.
Klaus said Wagner was putting the interests of the nation first by recommending deputies approve the draft in its first reading.
Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman, political enemy of Klaus, had demanded changes to the draft to curtail government authority over the budget once approved by parliament.

The Social Democrats (CSSD) at various times have also demanded a slowing in liberalisation of heating prices and state rents, a crackdown on tax evasion and economic crime, and more subsidies for the needy once prices are liberalised.
But the centre-left CSSD did not bring votes on these demands to the floor.

Klaus, welcoming signs of an opposition split, said on Wednesday: "I have expressed my disagreement with what Mr. Wagner said but I also want to appreciate Mr Wagner for suggesting...that the budget should go to a second reading."
With Senate elections due next month, the political climate is heating up. Klaus has repeatedly accused the Social Democrats of trying to reverse post-communist reforms.
